docs.title: EPICC: Epidemiological Cost Calculator
docs.text:
EPICC estimates what an outbreak costs, and what the public health response to it costs. It runs entirely in your browser: pick a model, adjust its parameters and scenarios, and read or export the report.

Open the app

The app is also deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud at https://epiworldpythonapp.streamlit.app/.

docs.title: In this documentation
docs.text:
• Models - every bundled model: what it estimates, its parameters with their sources, its scenarios and equations. Generated from the model files, so it always matches the app.
  • Sharing links - how the address bar records a calculation, and how to edit a link by hand.
  • Branding and themes - configuring the app's logo, fonts and colors.
  • Development - running EPICC locally, the checks, and building the static app and this site.
  • Versioning and releases - how versions and release notes work.
  • User stories - who EPICC is for and what is implemented.

EPICC is developed by ForeSITE at the University of Utah. The source is on GitHub; see CITATION.cff to cite it.

docs.title: Branding and themes
docs.text:
The app's identity is configured in src/epicc/config/default.yaml. This keeps the application title, logos, font stack, and light/dark color palettes together in one YAML file.

app:
  title: Epidemiological Cost Calculator (EPICC)

brand:
  name: ForeSITE
  font_family: '"Proxima Nova", "Avenir Next", Avenir, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif'
  logo:
    path: web/assets/foresite-primary-rgb.png
    dark_path: web/assets/foresite-white-rgb.png
    alt_text: ForeSITE logo
    mime_type: image/png
    width_px: 220
  colors: # Light mode
    primary: "#A60F2D"
    on_primary: "#FFFFFF"
    accent: "#FDB921"
    text: "#4E4E4E"
    muted_text: "#6B6E72"
    canvas: "#F7F7F5"
    surface: "#FFFFFF"
    border: "#D9D9D6"
    chart_palette: ["#A60F2D", "#FDB921", "#4E4E4E", "#6B6E72"]
  dark_colors: # Dark mode
    primary: "#FDB921"
    on_primary: "#231F20"
    accent: "#A60F2D"
    text: "#F3F1ED"
    muted_text: "#B8B3AD"
    canvas: "#171717"
    surface: "#242424"
    border: "#4E4E4E"
    chart_palette: ["#FDB921", "#A60F2D", "#F3F1ED", "#B8B3AD"]

colors controls the light palette and dark_colors controls the dark palette. Each needs the same semantic fields; on_primary is the text/icon color used on primary buttons. dark_colors and logo.dark_path are optional, so existing brand configurations continue to work and fall back to the light values.

Visitors choose System, Light, or Dark from Streamlit's menu in the top-right corner. The app mirrors that choice automatically, including switching to logo.dark_path when dark mode is active.

After changing branding, rebuild the static app before deployment:

make build

docs.title: Running EPICC locally
docs.text:
Install dependencies with a manager that reads pyproject.toml; the project uses uv:

uv sync
uv run -m streamlit run app.py

This step is not needed in the development container (.devcontainer/), which has everything installed.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text: Command What it runs make check lint, type check and tests; run it before opening a pull request make lint ruff make typecheck mypy make test pytest

docs.title: The static app
docs.text:
The public app is a static stlite build: Python runs in the visitor's browser, so there is no server.

make build    # -> dist/
make serve    # serve dist/ locally

docs.title: This website
docs.text:
The site is built with MkDocs and the Material theme from the Markdown in docs/. The model pages under Models are generated from the model files by scripts/build_model_docs.py and are not committed.

make docs          # generate the model pages and build the site -> site/
make docs-serve    # the same, served with live reload

The Pages workflow publishes the app at the site root and this documentation under /docs/. Pull requests build the site in strict mode, so a broken link or a missing page fails the check.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
The documentation is versioned with mike; the selector next to the title switches between versions.

Version Published when Contents 1.1.0, 1.2.0, ... a v* tag is pushed that release, permanently latest a v* tag is pushed alias of the newest release; /docs/ lands here dev every push to main the current main <version> (unreleased) a push to main whose version is not tagged yet replaced by the release

The app links to the documentation of its own version (app.docs_url contains {version}). The app on the site is built from main, so the unreleased entry makes sure that link works before the release exists.

scripts/deploy_docs.sh release|main does the publishing. Every version lives in its own folder on the docs-versions branch, which is the history: old versions are never rebuilt. Versions start at 1.1.0; earlier releases predate this site.

To document something, edit or add a Markdown page in docs/ and list it under nav in mkdocs.yml.

docs.title: Sharing links
docs.text:
The address bar is a permalink. As you change parameters the app rewrites the query string, so copying the URL is enough to hand someone the exact calculation you are looking at.

The query string is meant to be read — and edited — by hand:

https://epiworldpythonapp.streamlit.app/?model=measles&param.vaccination_rate=0.9&scen.22_cases.label=Small+outbreak&scen.22_cases.n_cases=30
Key Meaning model Which model to open, named by its YAML file stem (measles, measles_oregon, tb_isolation). Required. param.<parameter> An equation parameter value, keyed by its id in the model YAML. scen.<scenario>.<variable> A scenario variable, keyed by scenario id. scen.<scenario>.label A scenario's display label. scenarios Comma-separated scenario ids, in order. Only needed if you add, remove, or reorder scenarios.

Only values that differ from the model's defaults appear, so a link shows exactly what was changed and nothing else. Open a model without changing anything and the URL stays at ?model=measles.

Because links carry changes rather than a full snapshot, a link opened after the model's defaults change will pick up the new defaults for everything it does not mention. Use the parameter export (Save Changes as Preset) when you need a calculation pinned exactly.

Keys the app does not recognise are ignored. Values that cannot be honoured are reported with a warning in the app rather than failing silently: a number past its model-declared range is clamped to the range, while an unknown option, a fractional or browser-unsafe whole number, or a misspelled key is dropped. Equation parameters live under param., so even ids such as model, scenarios, embed, and embed_options cannot collide with the app's or Streamlit's top-level query keys. Write a parameter without that prefix and the app says so, rather than treating it as a stray key and leaving the default in place.

A model that isn't loaded in the browser — an uploaded one, or one from a newer version of the app — leaves its link pending with a warning; load that model and its values are applied then. If multiple loaded models use the same YAML filename, link sharing is disabled until the custom file is renamed, because its short URL name would be ambiguous. While you are trying unsaved edits from the model editor, the URL is also cleared: a link can carry parameter values but not the edits themselves, so it would reopen the saved model showing different numbers.

docs.title: Epidemiologist
docs.text:
1. As an epidemiologist, I want to select a disease so that all relevant costs are already populated.
  2. As an epidemiologist, I want to specify how many outbreak scenarios are included in the model so that it provides multiple points of comparison.
  3. As an epidemiologist, I want the app to include guardrails against generating misleading output, with a warning shown in worst-case scenarios.
  4. As an epidemiologist who is a heavy spreadsheet user, I want to author or edit model parameters in XLSX instead of hand-editing a YAML file, so the tool doesn't require technical file-format knowledge.
  5. As an epidemiologist, I want to download a documented parameter template (YAML or XLSX), specialize it with my own values, and load it back into the app.

Status: All of these are implemented. Nested columnar data may be worked with in YAML or XLSX (it all goes through the same code). All relevant costs are already populated per default values or presets as needed, and checked against a dynamically generated Pydantic model at update time to help ensure correctness.

docs.title: Public Health Official / SLTT Staff
docs.text:
1. As a public health official, I want to generate a report with a summary so I can share it directly with lawmakers, the general public, or other epidemiologists.
  2. As a public health official, I want to export that report as a PDF so I have a standard, print-ready format to distribute.
  3. As a public health official, I want to open a parameter file someone emailed me (YAML or XLSX) directly in Excel or a file previewer, without launching the app, just to see what's in it before deciding to load it.

Status: Report generation is not yet complete (at least as far as DOCX is concerned). Reports can be exported as PDF, but the output quality and formatting are still limited. EPICC does not need to add functionality for previewing parameter files, since this is handled by standard OS and spreadsheet tooling.

docs.title: Any User
docs.text:
1. As any user, I want to save the current state of the model so I can share it and reuse it later.
  2. As any user, I want to reload a previously saved or shared parameter file back into the app.
  3. As any user, I want to read the assumptions behind the model (a longer description, not just numbers) so I can justify the figures to others.
  4. As any user, I want my in-progress configuration to persist if I accidentally close or refresh the app, so I don't lose my work.
  5. Unsure the best way to do this.
  6. As any user authoring my own parameter file, I want clear validation error messages when the file is malformed or missing required fields, so I can fix it myself.

Status: Yes, exporting/importing is a common feature throughout the cost calculator. Model parameters may include help text and references to aid in future understanding and documentation. All is checked against a dynamically generated Pydantic model at update time to help ensure correctness.

docs.title: Developer
docs.text:
1. As a developer, I want the app to be modular so I can extend it easily to other diseases.
  2. As a developer, I want a unified read/write abstraction across parameter formats (YAML, XLSX, and future formats like CSV), so adding a new format later doesn't require rebuilding the validation layer.

Status: The app is modular, and so is the parameter loading system.

docs.title: Versioning and releases
docs.text:
The project follows Semantic Versioning. The current version appears next to the title in the app header, and the What's new button links to the latest release.

Release notes are not kept in the repository. GitHub generates them from the pull requests merged since the previous release, so the only thing that shapes them is how you title your PRs. To cut a release:

make bump BUMP=minor          # or BUMP=patch / BUMP=major, or VERSION=1.2.3

That updates the version in src/epicc/__init__.py and pyproject.toml, then prints the commands to finish:

release_version=1.2.3       # replace with the version printed by make bump
git commit -am "Release v${release_version}"
git tag -a "v${release_version}" -m "v${release_version}"
git push --follow-tags

Pushing the tag triggers release.yml, which publishes the GitHub release with generated notes. The app's What's new link then points at it with no further action. make test fails if pyproject.toml and epicc.__version__ ever disagree, and the release workflow refuses a tag that does not match the source.

docs.title: Measles Outbreak Cost Estimation
docs.text:
Estimates hospitalization, tracing, and productivity costs for measles outbreaks across three outbreak-size scenarios.

Authors: Edward Wang, Olivia Banks, George G. Vega Yon, Richard Nelson

Model id: measles. Open it in the app with ?model=measles; see Sharing links.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This calculator estimates the economic burden of measles outbreaks by modeling three key cost components: direct medical costs (hospitalization), indirect costs (lost productivity from quarantine), and public health response costs (contact tracing).

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
The model evaluates three outbreak scenarios based on historical U.S. measles outbreaks:

  • 22 Cases: Small outbreak (typical in high-vaccination areas)
  • 100 Cases: Medium outbreak
  • 803 Cases: Large outbreak (similar to 2019 U.S. outbreak)

docs.title: Key Assumptions
docs.text:
• All costs are in USD
  • Hospitalization rate and costs based on CDC surveillance data
  • Contact tracing effort scales linearly with case count
  • Lost productivity only counts quarantined unvaccinated contacts
  • Wage figures represent average hourly earnings

docs.title: Measles Outbreak Costs in Oregon
docs.text:
What a measles outbreak costs Oregon, using three real Oregon outbreak sizes and Oregon-specific vaccination coverage and wages.

Authors: George G. Vega Yon

Model id: measles_oregon. Open it in the app with ?model=measles_oregon; see Sharing links.

docs.title: What this estimates
docs.text:
What one measles outbreak costs Oregon, across three sizes Oregon has actually seen: an early 5-case cluster, the 31 cases of 2024, and the 45 cases confirmed so far in 2026.

Cost is split three ways:

  1. Public health response - a fixed cost to stand up the response, plus staff time per case.
  2. Lost work during quarantine - susceptible contacts sent home for 21 days.
  3. Medical care - hospitalizations, clinic visits, and lab tests.

The lever that matters is MMR coverage among exposed contacts. Every immune contact is one fewer person in quarantine, so coverage scales the largest cost component directly.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
• All costs in 2025-2026 USD, from a societal perspective.
  • Contacts are traced and quarantined at the same rate for every case.
  • A lost workday is valued at 8 hours of the Oregon average wage.
  • Long-term costs (SSPE, deaths, lost school days) are not counted, so these are conservative.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Oregon Health Authority, student immunization rates, May 2026.
  • Oregon Health Authority measles case counts (31 in 2024; 45 as of Aug 13, 2026).
  • Pike et al. (2021), Societal Costs of a Measles Outbreak, Pediatrics 147(4).
  • Johns Hopkins IVAC, Vaccine (2025), review of U.S. measles outbreak costs, 2000-2025.
  • CDC measles surveillance, 2026 year to date.
  • U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics OEWS, May 2025; Oregon Employment Department, 2025.

Evaluated in order; each can use the parameters and any equation above it.

Lost work during quarantine (USD) eq_quarantine_loss

docs.title: TB Isolation Cost Estimation
docs.text:
Estimates hospitalization, tracing, and productivity costs for TB isolation scenarios, comparing 14-day vs. 5-day isolation protocols.

Authors: Edward Wang, Olivia Banks

Model id: tb_isolation. Open it in the app with ?model=tb_isolation; see Sharing links.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This calculator compares the economic impact of two tuberculosis isolation protocols: 14-day isolation (standard) versus 5-day isolation (shortened). The model accounts for direct isolation costs, lost productivity, and the long-term costs of secondary TB infections.

$$ \text{LaTeX test.} $$

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
• 14-day Isolation: Standard isolation protocol for infectious TB patients
  • 5-day Isolation: Shortened isolation protocol (increases secondary transmission risk)

docs.title: Key Model Components
docs.text:
1. Secondary Infection Estimation: Models latent and active TB cases resulting from reduced isolation time
  2. Direct Costs: Daily costs vary by isolation setting (hospital, motel, or home)
  3. Productivity Loss: Lost wages during isolation period (index case only)
  4. Secondary Infection Costs: Long-term costs of treating latent and active TB in contacts, with appropriate discounting over remaining years of life

docs.title: Transmission Risk Impact
docs.text: Reducing isolation duration increases the infectious period, leading to more secondary cases:

docs.title: Economic Impact Summary
docs.text:
The trade-off between isolation duration and transmission risk creates complex economic dynamics:

  • Short-term savings: Reduced isolation costs and productivity losses
  • Long-term costs: Higher burden from secondary infections
  • Net effect: Often favors longer isolation from a societal cost perspective

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
• All costs are in USD
  • Shortened isolation increases infectiousness by a multiplier
  • Latent TB progression to active disease occurs in two phases: first 2 years and remainder of lifetime
  • Future costs are discounted at the specified discount rate
  • Productivity loss assumes 8-hour workdays

docs.title: Equations
docs.text:
Evaluated in order; each can use the parameters and any equation above it.

Baseline latent TB infections (cases) eq_latent_baseline

contacts_per_case * prob_latent_if_14_day

Latent TB infections (cases) eq_latent

eq_latent_baseline * latent_multiplier

Active TB disease (cases) eq_active

eq_latent * prob_latent_to_active_2yr + eq_latent * (1 - prob_latent_to_active_2yr) * prob_latent_to_active_lifetime

Daily isolation cost (USD/day) eq_daily_cost

(direct_medical_cost_day if (isolation_type == "HOSP_ISO" and direct_medical_cost_day > 0) else (isolation_cost if isolation_type == "HOSP_ISO" else (motel_room_cost + hourly_wage_nurse * nurse_checkin_hours if isolation_type == "MOTEL_ISO" else hourly_wage_nurse * nurse_checkin_hours)))

Direct cost of isolation (USD) eq_direct

eq_daily_cost * isolation_days

Lost productivity (USD) eq_productivity

isolation_days * workday_ratio * hourly_wage_worker * 8

Discounted 2-year progression probability (dimensionless) eq_discounted_2yr

(prob_latent_to_active_2yr / 2) / ((1 + discount_rate) ** 1) + (prob_latent_to_active_2yr / 2) / ((1 + discount_rate) ** 2)

Cost per latent case (with discounting) (USD) eq_secondary_cost_per_latent

cost_latent + cost_active * (eq_discounted_2yr + sum((prob_latent_to_active_lifetime / remaining_years_of_life) / ((1 + discount_rate) ** y) for y in range(3, remaining_years_of_life + 1)))

Cost of secondary infections (USD) eq_secondary

eq_latent * eq_secondary_cost_per_latent

Total cost (USD) eq_total

eq_direct + eq_productivity + eq_secondary
